sourceNotes: Every dated entry was read from the cited source on its sourceCheckedOn date. endoflife.date aggregates vendor lifecycle pages; entries sourced from it carry confidence "aggregator" and should be re-confirmed against the vendor page before a date drives a maintenance window. Refresh procedure: .claude/skills/polaris-tech-lifecycle/references/eol-dataset.md. The 2026-09-09 pass moved five families to current versions (PostgreSQL 15->17, Java 17->25, Go 1.22->1.26/1.27, nginx mainline->stable 1.30, the Debian image base 12->13) and re-read the vendor pages for each rather than trusting the aggregator, which is why several entries carry confidence vendor now.

technologies.label: Node.js
technologies.notes: Even majors become LTS in the October after release; odd majors never do and die at ~7 months. Polaris targets an LTS line only. minimum is 22 because that is the dependency tree's actual floor (engines.node is >=22.12.0), NOT what gets provisioned - every install path installs 24, and the accept-checks tolerate 22 or 24. So a host on the floor is supported but has under a year of runway, since 22 dies 2027-04-30. Target and maximumTested are both 24: it is what CI runs and what every script installs.

technologies.label: PostgreSQL
technologies.notes: Five-year support policy; a major dies in the November of its fifth year. Moved 15 -> 17 on 2026-09-09: TimescaleDB 2.29 dropped PostgreSQL 15, so staying on 15 capped the extension at the 2.28.x line. 17 rather than 18 because 17 is what the Debian trixie image base ships as postgresql-client-17, so the container needs no PGDG apt repo of its own; TimescaleDB 2.30 is packaged for both. Every install path now provisions it from PGDG on Debian/Ubuntu too - the distro metapackage was 14 on 22.04 and 16 on 24.04, never the stated major, and had no number in its name for the pin check to catch.

tracks.note: Polaris's major until 2026-09-09; last one supported by the TimescaleDB 2.28.x line.
Polaris's minimum and target. Debian 13 (trixie) ships this major, which is what the container image uses as its client.

technologies.label: TimescaleDB
technologies.notes: TimescaleDB publishes no dated end-of-life for its own minors. Its lifecycle is a PostgreSQL-compatibility horizon instead: 2.28.x is the last line supporting PostgreSQL 15, and 2.29.0 supports only 16/17/18. That horizon is what drove the PostgreSQL 15 -> 17 move on 2026-09-09; 2.30.0 is the current line and is packaged for 17. Graded informational - the actionable fact lives on the PostgreSQL row and in the postgres-major playbook.

technologies.label: Go toolchain
technologies.notes: Go supports only the two most recent majors: a release dies the day the major two ahead of it ships. Build-time only on a Polaris host (the in-app agent build), never in the serving path, so an EOL toolchain grades warning rather than critical. Moved off the long-EOL 1.22 floor on 2026-09-09. Minimum 1.26 and target 1.27 are two numbers on purpose, the same arrangement as Node: 1.26 and 1.27 are the two supported majors, and no Linux path can install 1.27 today - the RHEL go-toolset module carries 1.26.7 and the Go snap's newest channel is 1.26/stable - while the Windows scripts pin 1.27.0, the newest winget has a manifest for. Neither Ubuntu LTS can satisfy the floor from its archive at all (24.04 ships 1.22, 22.04 ships 1.18), so the snap fallback is the branch that runs there.

tracks.note: Polaris's floor until 2026-09-09, long past upstream support by then.
Polaris's floor - the older of the two supported majors, and the newest the RHEL go-toolset module and the Go snap carry.
Current release; what the Windows scripts pin (1.27.0, the newest winget manifest).

technologies.label: nginx
technologies.notes: Odd minors are mainline, even minors are stable; a branch dies when its successor of the same parity ships. The floor was 1.25 for a long time because that is the first branch with stable HTTP/3 - a FEATURE requirement, and 1.25 itself went EOL 2024-05-29. On 2026-09-09 the Linux setup scripts moved from the nginx.org mainline repository to the STABLE one and the floor became 1.30, the oldest branch still receiving fixes, so the number is now a support statement. The mainline stanza is still written into the repo file at enabled=0 for anyone who needs a newer feature.

tracks.note: First branch with stable HTTP/3; Polaris's documented floor.
Current stable - Polaris's floor and what the setup scripts install (1.30.4 on 2026-09-09).
Current mainline; what the disabled mainline stanza and nginx:mainline resolve to.

technologies.label: Java (Microsoft Build of OpenJDK)
technologies.notes: Only needed to run jsign for agent code signing, so build-time only. The deploy scripts install Microsoft.OpenJDK.25 on Windows, java-25-openjdk-headless on RHEL and openjdk-25-jre-headless on Debian/Ubuntu and in the container image; these dates are Microsoft's build, which can differ from Oracle's and Temurin's for the same major. TARGET ALWAYS EQUALS MINIMUM here, and that rule survived the move: a target above what every install path provisions makes every healthy install report a behind-target Java forever, which is noise that teaches operators to ignore this card. It was 21-with-a-17-minimum briefly and that was the mistake. Moved 17 -> 25 on 2026-09-09 as the current LTS - jsign 7.5 is Java 8 bytecode (class file major 52) and requires none of it, so this buys runway (2030-09-30 rather than 2027-09-30) rather than capability. Availability was checked on every path before moving, since one platform without the package would have split the fleet's signing JDK again: RHEL 9 AppStream, Debian trixie, Ubuntu 22.04 AND 24.04, winget, and the aka.ms MSI all carry 25.

tracks.note: Current LTS - Polaris's minimum and target.

technologies.label: RHEL / Rocky / AlmaLinux
technologies.notes: eol here is the end of Maintenance Support (security patches stop); activeSupportEnds is the end of Full Support (no new hardware enablement or non-critical fixes after it). Rocky and AlmaLinux track the same majors on the same calendar.

technologies.label: Ubuntu
technologies.notes: LTS only - Polaris does not support interim Ubuntu releases. extendedSupport is Ubuntu Pro ESM, which requires a subscription; do not treat it as free runway.

technologies.label: Debian
technologies.notes: Reported as "Container base image" rather than a host OS when Polaris runs in a container - the Dockerfile is built FROM node:24-trixie, which is Debian 13 (moved from bookworm on 2026-09-09: trixie ships the PostgreSQL 17 client and openjdk-25, so neither needs a third-party repo inside the image). extendedSupport is the volunteer LTS project, not the Debian security team.

tracks.note: bookworm - the Docker base image until 2026-09-09.

technologies.label: Windows Server
technologies.notes: Deliberately ungraded. os.release() reports a build number (10.0.20348 for 2022, 10.0.26100 for 2025) and the build-to-product table rots; Windows Server lifecycles are also ~10 years, which is not the risk this feature exists to catch. The observed build is reported on the card for reference only.

technologies.label: Prisma
technologies.notes: Prisma publishes no end-of-life dates for its majors, so there is nothing to grade against a calendar - an out-of-date major is upgrade debt, not an EOL risk. Reported so the card shows the full stack. npm audit has advised downgrading Prisma 7 here; that advice is wrong (see the dependency-audit reference).

technologies.label: PgBouncer
technologies.notes: PgBouncer publishes no dated lifecycle. Polaris also cannot detect its version: that needs SHOW VERSION on the admin console (port 6432, pgbouncer database, an admin user) with credentials Polaris does not hold. Presence is detected; the version is reported undetectable and the operator is asked to confirm the 1.21+ floor by hand.

technologies.label: etcd (HA only)
technologies.notes: Present only on an active/standby HA install (docs/HA.md); a single-node Polaris has no etcd. The VENDOR page states a rule, not dates: 'The etcd project maintains release branches for the current version and previous release. For example, when v3.5 is the current version, v3.4 is supported. When v3.6 is released, v3.4 goes out of support.' That is why policy is compat - a track can fall out of support because something NEW shipped, with no date announced in advance, so this entry cannot warn ahead of time the way a dated family does. The per-track dates below come from endoflife.date, not from etcd, hence confidence aggregator. Polaris pins no etcd version anywhere: deploy/ha/setup-rhel-ha.sh runs `dnf --enablerepo=pgdg-rhel9-extras install -y etcd`, so the version is whatever PGDG ships and it can change under a fresh standby build. The 3.5 floor is the etcd3 API the Patroni template targets (deploy/ha/patroni.yml.example, etcd3.hosts), and target equals minimum deliberately: nothing about a newer etcd is needed, and 3.5 has the longest announced support of any current track. maximumTested 3.5 is generous - NO etcd version has been exercised on real hardware, because deploy/ha has never run on a real pair. DRAFT: polarisMinimum/Target need a human decision, per the skill's human-review rule.

tracks.note: Went out of support when 3.6 shipped. Date is endoflife.date's, not an etcd announcement.

Kept alive well past the two-branch rule - endoflife.date shows support to 2027-07-08 and a 3.5.33 patch. Recorded as a plain eol, not extendedSupport: that field takes the date an extended phase ENDS, and no separate date for the end of 3.5's normal support was published to put in eol alongside it. Polaris's floor.
Current branch, so 3.5 is now the older of the two supported ones only by virtue of its extended support.

technologies.label: Patroni (HA only)
technologies.notes: Present only on an active/standby HA install (docs/HA.md). Patroni publishes NO dated lifecycle: its docs and GitHub carry release notes and a supported-PostgreSQL matrix, but no supported-version or end-of-life policy, and a search on 2026-09-09 found none - hence policy none and confidence aggregator rather than a vendor read of a policy that does not exist. In practice only the newest release gets fixes. Polaris pins no version: deploy/ha/setup-rhel-ha.sh runs `dnf install -y patroni patroni-etcd` from PGDG, so a standby built today can land on a different major than the primary. The 3 floor is what deploy/ha/patroni.yml.example was written against; 4.x is ANTICIPATED rather than unsupported - the on_role_change callback ignores the role Patroni passes and re-derives it from the REST API precisely because the role vocabulary changed between 3.x and 4.x. Upstream is 4.1.5 as of 2026-09. No Patroni version has run on real hardware. DRAFT: the floor and whether to state a 4.x target need a human decision.

playbooks.title: Move etcd or Patroni on an HA pair
steps: Neither is pinned by this repo: both come unversioned from PGDG, so decide the target version first and install it explicitly rather than letting `dnf install` choose per host.
Both nodes must match. A version skew between primary and standby is the failure this pair is most likely to hit, because a standby rebuilt months later gets whatever PGDG ships that day.
Patroni first or etcd first is not arbitrary: upgrade etcd across all THREE members (both database nodes and the witness) one at a time, confirming quorum between each, before touching Patroni.
etcd supports only the current and previous release branch, so plan a move before the branch in use falls out of support - there is no announced date to wait for.
Re-check the role callback after any Patroni major: it re-derives the role from the REST API because the vocabulary changed in 4.x, and that is the seam a major would break.
Rehearse a switchover before trusting the pair again, per the drills in docs/HA.md.

playbooks.title: Move Polaris to a new Node major
steps: Confirm the target major is an LTS line and its own EOL is at least 12 months out.
Bump engines.node and @types/node in package.json, then npm install to refresh the lockfile.
Bump the FROM lines in Dockerfile (builder and runtime) and Dockerfile.dev.
Widen the node -v accept-check and the install source in all four Linux setup scripts.
Bump the pinned version and the MSI fallback URL in both Windows setup scripts.
Bump node-version in both workflow files.
Update the supported-versions table in docs/INSTALL.md, README.md and the CLAUDE.md tech-stack row.
Run npm run check:versions, then typecheck, lint and the full suite against a real database.

playbooks.title: Move Polaris to a new PostgreSQL major
steps: Check the TimescaleDB package for the target major exists (timescaledb-2-postgresql-N) before planning anything else.
Take a verified backup and confirm a restore into a scratch database first.
Install the target major side by side from PGDG, then pg_upgrade (or dump/restore for a small install).

On Docker, steps 3 and 5-7 do not apply: the image carries one major's binaries, so it is dump then restore into a NEW container with a NEW data directory, with the old container kept as the rollback. A tag swap over the existing data directory refuses to start, and a copy of the old appdata restores only back into the old major. See docs/INSTALL.md - On Docker / Unraid, where PostgreSQL is its own container.

On Docker, remember a new data directory is a new postgresql.conf: ssl and max_connections revert to the image defaults, and both are set as container arguments (-c ssl=on -c max_connections=N), not in a file the image keeps. If the old container had TLS and the new one does not, the unchanged DATABASE_URL fails on 'The server does not support SSL connections'.
Re-run the timescaledb extension update and confirm every hypertable and chunk survived.

Rewrite the per-host drop-in /etc/systemd/system/<unit>.d/20-postgres.conf with the new unit name - the SHIPPED units name no PostgreSQL unit and must not be edited. On Windows, the service name and the bin-path probe list.
Bump PG_MAJOR / PG_CLIENT_MAJOR in every setup script (RHEL, Ubuntu and both -nodb variants), plus the installer pin on Windows. All four are checked by check:versions.

Bump the image tags in compose.dev.yml and the CI service container, and postgresql-client-<major> in BOTH Dockerfiles - the image base must actually ship that major, or add the PGDG apt repo to the image.
Smoke-test the backup and restore path end to end - it is the only code that calls timescaledb_pre_restore and post_restore.

playbooks.title: Move the TimescaleDB extension
steps: Read the chunk-bloat runbook first - a version move and a chunk-interval change should not land together.
Confirm the target extension version still supports the running PostgreSQL major (2.29 dropped 15).
Take a verified backup; the restore path has extension-version-sensitive gates.
Update the package, restart PostgreSQL, then ALTER EXTENSION timescaledb UPDATE.
Confirm every hypertable, chunk interval and retention policy survived, and that CI's non-Timescale Postgres has not masked a regression.

playbooks.title: Move a Polaris host to a new OS major
steps: Prefer a rebuild onto the new major over an in-place distro upgrade; Polaris installs cleanly from the setup script.
Check the nginx.org repository URL for the new major - the baseurl encodes the OS release, so a RHEL 10 move is a URL change, not just a doc change.
Confirm the PGDG and TimescaleDB repositories publish for the new major.
Re-run the setup script on a scratch host and diff the resulting unit files against the shipped ones.
Restore a production backup onto the new host and compare the capacity snapshot before cutting over.

playbooks.title: Move the nginx floor
steps: Decide mainline or stable: since 2026-09-09 the setup scripts install the nginx.org STABLE branch, with the mainline stanza written at enabled=0.
Widen the accept-regex in all four Linux setup scripts and the migrate-to-nginx helper.
Update the >= claims in docs/INSTALL.md, which state the floor three times.
Re-apply the managed config and confirm HTTP/3 still negotiates.

playbooks.title: Move the Java major used for agent signing
steps: Confirm the jsign release in use runs on the target major (7.5 is Java 8 bytecode, so anything from 8 up), and that the JDK package EXISTS on every platform - RHEL AppStream, Debian, both Ubuntu LTSes, winget and the aka.ms MSI. One platform without it splits the fleet's signing JDK.
Bump the JDK package in the Dockerfile and the winget id plus MSI URL in every setup script.

Bump JAVA_MINIMUM in src/services/agentSigningService.ts - the number the running app states. Both signingAvailability error strings interpolate it and the Code-signing card renders availability.javaMinimum, so the browser carries no literal of its own. check:versions reads it, and it is the only Java site inside src/.
Re-sign one agent binary and verify the signature chain before shipping.

playbooks.title: Move the Go pin for the agent toolchain
steps: Bump the go directive in agent/go.mod and run go mod tidy in agent/.
Bump GO_MINIMUM in the agent build service so the preflight check and every copy string move together.
Widen the go version accept-regex in all four Linux setup scripts and bump both Windows winget ids and MSI URLs.
Check whether the Dockerfile still needs the backports pin for golang-go.
Bump agent/VERSION and rebuild every platform binary - the agent version and the shipped binaries move in lockstep.
Re-sign the binaries and confirm an existing agent upgrades cleanly.

playbooks.title: Move to a new Prisma major
steps: Read the Prisma client lifecycle cross-cutting reference before touching the version.
Bump prisma, @prisma/client and @prisma/adapter-pg together - they are one version.
Re-run prisma generate and typecheck; the generated client is gitignored, so every checkout regenerates.
Replay every migration against a scratch database, then run the integration suite against a real Postgres.
Ignore any npm audit advice to downgrade the major.
